'''Mei Hong''' (born 1970) is a [[Chinese-American]] biophysical chemist and professor of chemistry at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://meihonglab.com/professor-mei-hong/|title=Professor Mei Hong – Hong Lab MIT|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-21}}</ref> She is known for her creative development and application of [[solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance]] (ssNMR) spectroscopy to elucidate the structures and mechanisms of [[membrane protein]]s, plant [[cell wall]]s, and [[amyloid]] proteins. She has received a number of recognitions for her work, including the American Chemical Society Nakanishi Prize in 2021, [[Günther Laukien Prize]] in 2014,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Ernst|first=Richard R.|date=April 2005|title=The Günther Laukien Prize|journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance|volume=173|issue=2|pages=188–191|bibcode=2005JMagR.173..188E|doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2005.02.006|issn=1090-7807|pmid=15780911}}</ref> the Protein Society Young Investigator award in 2012, and the American Chemical Society’s Pure Chemistry award in 2003.

== Education and career ==
Hong grew up in China and completed her B.A. degree in chemistry from [[Mount Holyoke College]] (''[[summa cum laude]]'') in 1992 and a Ph.D. degree from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1996. There she worked in the laboratory of [[Alexander Pines]] to investigate phospholipid structure and dynamics using variable-angle-spinning NMR. After a one-year postdoctoral stint in the laboratory of [[Robert G. Griffin]] at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, she went to [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]] and developed biosynthetic isotopic labeling approaches to advance protein structure determination by ssNMR. She started an assistant professorship at [[Iowa State University]] in 1999, became an associate professor in 2002 and full professor in 2004, and held the first [[John Corbett (chemist)|John D. Corbett]] Professorship from 2007 to 2010. In 2014, she returned to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a professor of chemistry.<ref name=":0" />

== Research ==
Hong's research focuses on elucidating the structure, dynamics and mechanism of membrane proteins using ssNMR. She is particularly known for her in-depth study of the [[M2 proton channel|Matrix-2 (M2) proteins]] of [[influenza A virus]]es, which are responsible for all [[Influenza pandemic|flu pandemics]] in history. M2 is an acid-activated proton channel and a membrane scission protein of the influenza virus.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hong|first1=Mei|last2=DeGrado|first2=William F.|date=2012-10-09|title=Structural basis for proton conduction and inhibition by the influenza M2 protein|journal=Protein Science|volume=21|issue=11|pages=1620–1633|doi=10.1002/pro.2158|pmid=23001990|pmc=3527700}}</ref> Hong's ssNMR studies have provided insights into the proton-conduction mechanism of this channel, by quantifying the proton transfer rates and [[Dynamic equilibrium|equilibria]] between water and the proton-selective [[histidine]] residue.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hu|first1=F.|last2=Luo|first2=W.|last3=Hong|first3=M.|date=2010-10-21|title=Mechanisms of Proton Conduction and Gating in Influenza M2 Proton Channels from Solid-State NMR|journal=Science|volume=330|issue=6003|pages=505–508|doi=10.1126/science.1191714|pmid=20966251|issn=0036-8075|pmc=4102303|bibcode=2010Sci...330..505H}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hu|first1=Fanghao|last2=Schmidt-Rohr|first2=Klaus|last3=Hong|first3=Mei|date=2011-10-21|title=NMR Detection of pH-Dependent Histidine–Water Proton Exchange Reveals the Conduction Mechanism of a Transmembrane Proton Channel|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=134|issue=8|pages=3703–3713|doi=10.1021/ja2081185|pmid=21974716|issn=0002-7863|pmc=3288706}}</ref> She showed that the antiviral drug [[amantadine]] inhibits proton conduction by direct occlusion of the channel pore.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cady|first1=Sarah D.|last2=Schmidt-Rohr|first2=Klaus|last3=Wang|first3=Jun|last4=Soto|first4=Cinque S.|last5=DeGrado|first5=William F.|last6=Hong|first6=Mei|date=2010|title=Structure of the amantadine binding site of influenza M2 proton channels in lipid bilayers|journal=Nature|volume=463|issue=7281|pages=689–692|doi=10.1038/nature08722|pmid=20130653|issn=0028-0836|pmc=2818718|bibcode=2010Natur.463..689C}}</ref> She determined the [[cholesterol]]-binding structure of the M2 protein, which sheds light on how cholesterol mediates M2's membrane scission function.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Elkins|first1=Matthew R.|last2=Williams|first2=Jonathan K.|last3=Gelenter|first3=Martin D.|last4=Dai|first4=Peng|last5=Kwon|first5=Byungsu|last6=Sergeyev|first6=Ivan V.|last7=Pentelute|first7=Bradley L.|last8=Hong|first8=Mei|date=2017-11-20|title=Cholesterol-binding site of the influenza M2 protein in lipid bilayers from solid-state NMR|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=114|issue=49|pages=12946–12951|doi=10.1073/pnas.1715127114|pmid=29158386|pmc=5724280|bibcode=2017PNAS..11412946E |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2020 she determined both the influenza B M2 protein structure<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mandala|first1=Venkata S.|last2=Loftis|first2=Alexander R.|last3=Shcherbakov|first3=Alexander A.|last4=Pentelute|first4=Bradley L.|last5=Hong|first5=Mei|date=2020-02-03|title=Atomic structures of closed and open influenza B M2 proton channel reveal the conduction mechanism|url= |journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology|language=en|volume=27|issue=2|pages=160–167|doi=10.1038/s41594-019-0371-2|pmid=32015551|pmc=7641042|s2cid=211017938|issn=1545-9985}}</ref> and the SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein structure,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mandala|first1=Venkata S.|last2=McKay|first2=Matthew J.|last3=Shcherbakov|first3=Alexander A.|last4=Dregni|first4=Aurelio J.|last5=Kolocouris|first5=Antonios|last6=Hong|first6=Mei|date=December 2020|title=Structure and drug binding of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein transmembrane domain in lipid bilayers|journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology|language=en|volume=27|issue=12|pages=1202–1208|doi=10.1038/s41594-020-00536-8|pmid=33177698|pmc=7718435|issn=1545-9985|doi-access=free}}</ref> the latter in rapid response to COVID-19. The 1.5 Å BM2 structures in the closed and open states revealed different activation mechanisms of BM2 compared to influenza AM2. The 2.1 Å SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein structure forms the basis for antiviral drug design.

Other membrane proteins that Hong's group has studied include [[Beta hairpin|β-hairpin]] [[antimicrobial peptides]],<ref name=":3" /> channel-forming [[colicin]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Luo|first1=Wenbin|last2=Yao|first2=Xiaolan|last3=Hong|first3=Mei|date=2005|title=Large Structure Rearrangement of Colicin Ia Channel Domain after Membrane Binding from 2D13C Spin Diffusion NMR|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=127|issue=17|pages=6402–6408|doi=10.1021/ja0433121|pmid=15853348|bibcode=2005JAChS.127.6402L |issn=0002-7863}}</ref> and [[Membrane fusion protein|viral fusion proteins]].<ref name=":4" /> She determined the structure of the membrane toroidal pores formed by the antimicrobial peptide [[Protegrin|protegrin-1]],<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Mani|first1=R.|last2=Cady|first2=S. D.|last3=Tang|first3=M.|last4=Waring|first4=A. J.|last5=Lehrer|first5=R. I.|last6=Hong|first6=M.|date=2006-10-23|title=Membrane-dependent oligomeric structure and pore formation of a beta-hairpin antimicrobial peptide in lipid bilayers from solid-state NMR|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=103|issue=44|pages=16242–16247|doi=10.1073/pnas.0605079103|pmid=17060626|issn=0027-8424|bibcode=2006PNAS..10316242M|pmc=1637567|doi-access=free }}</ref> which explained the membrane-disruptive mechanism of this peptide. She showed that the [[transmembrane domain]] of viral fusion proteins can be conformationally plastic, and the [[Beta sheet|β-sheet]] conformation can correlate with the generation of membrane curvature and membrane dehydration, which are necessary for [[Viral entry|virus-cell fusion]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Yao|first1=Hongwei|last2=Lee|first2=Michelle W.|last3=Waring|first3=Alan J.|last4=Wong|first4=Gerard C. L.|last5=Hong|first5=Mei|date=2015-08-17|title=Viral fusion protein transmembrane domain adopts β-strand structure to facilitate membrane topological changes for virus–cell fusion|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=112|issue=35|pages=10926–10931|doi=10.1073/pnas.1501430112|pmid=26283363|issn=0027-8424|bibcode=2015PNAS..11210926Y|pmc=4568205|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Hong has also investigated the structure and dynamics of amyloid proteins, including full-length tau<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dregni|first1=Aurelio J.|last2=Mandala|first2=Venkata S.|last3=Wu|first3=Haifan|last4=Elkins|first4=Matthew R.|last5=Wang|first5=Harrison K.|last6=Hung|first6=Ivan|last7=DeGrado|first7=William F.|last8=Hong|first8=Mei|date=2019-08-13|title=In vitro 0N4R tau fibrils contain a monomorphic β-sheet core enclosed by dynamically heterogeneous fuzzy coat segments|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=116|issue=33|pages=16357–16366|doi=10.1073/pnas.1906839116|issn=0027-8424|pmid=31358628|pmc=6697781|bibcode=2019PNAS..11616357D |doi-access=free}}</ref> and Aβ peptides involved in [[Neurodegeneration|neurodegenerative]] diseases<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Elkins|first1=Matthew R.|last2=Wang|first2=Tuo|last3=Nick|first3=Mimi|last4=Jo|first4=Hyunil|last5=Lemmin|first5=Thomas|last6=Prusiner|first6=Stanley B.|last7=DeGrado|first7=William F.|last8=Stöhr|first8=Jan|last9=Hong|first9=Mei|date=2016-07-28|title=Structural Polymorphism of Alzheimer's β-Amyloid Fibrils as Controlled by an E22 Switch: A Solid-State NMR Study|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=138|issue=31|pages=9840–9852|doi=10.1021/jacs.6b03715|pmid=27414264|issn=0002-7863|hdl=1721.1/113318|pmc=5149419|bibcode=2016JAChS.138.9840E }}</ref> as well as amyloid fibrils formed by designed peptides.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Zinc-Binding Structure of a Catalytic Amyloid from Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy|last1=Lee|first1=M.|last2=Wang|first2=T.|date=2017-05-31|last3=Makhlynets|first3=O.V.|last4=Wu|first4=Y.|last5=Polizzi|first5=N.|last6=Wu|first6=H.|last7=Gosavi|first7=P.M.|last8=Korendovych|first8=I.V.|last9=DeGrado|first9=W.F.|doi = 10.2210/pdb5ugk/pdb}}</ref> She showed that the peptide hormone glucagon fibrillizes into an antiparallel hydrogen-bonded β-sheet with two coexisting molecular conformations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gelenter|first1=Martin D.|last2=Smith|first2=Katelyn J.|last3=Liao|first3=Shu-Yu|last4=Mandala|first4=Venkata S.|last5=Dregni|first5=Aurelio J.|last6=Lamm|first6=Matthew S.|last7=Tian|first7=Yu|last8=Pochan|first8=Darrin J.|last9=Tucker|first9=Thomas J.|last10=Su|first10=Yongchao|last11=Hong|first11=Mei|date=2019-06-24|title=The peptide hormone glucagon forms amyloid fibrils with two coexisting β-strand conformations|journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology|language=en|volume=26|issue=7|pages=592–598|doi=10.1038/s41594-019-0238-6|pmid=31235909|pmc=6609468|issn=1545-9985|hdl=1721.1/125383|hdl-access=free}}</ref> These studies shed light on the origin of structural polymorphism, water interaction,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Tuo|last2=Jo|first2=Hyunil|last3=DeGrado|first3=William F.|last4=Hong|first4=Mei|date=2017-04-21|title=Water Distribution, Dynamics, and Interactions with Alzheimer's β-Amyloid Fibrils Investigated by Solid-State NMR|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=139|issue=17|pages=6242–6252|doi=10.1021/jacs.7b02089|pmid=28406028|issn=0002-7863|pmc=5808936|bibcode=2017JAChS.139.6242W }}</ref> and metal ion binding.

Hong pioneered the study of plant [[cell wall]]s using multidimensional ssNMR.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Tuo|last2=Hong|first2=Mei|date=2015-09-09|title=Solid-state NMR investigations of cellulose structure and interactions with matrix polysaccharides in plant primary cell walls|journal=Journal of Experimental Botany|volume=67|issue=2|pages=503–514|doi=10.1093/jxb/erv416|pmid=26355148|pmc=6280985|issn=0022-0957}}</ref> These studies revealed the molecular interactions of the [[polysaccharide]]s in plant cell walls, and helped to revise the conventional model of the primary cell wall structure by proposing a single-network model where [[cellulose]], [[hemicellulose]] and [[pectin]]s all interact with each other.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pérez García|first1=Marilú|last2=Zhang|first2=Yuan|last3=Hayes|first3=Jennifer|last4=Salazar|first4=Andre|last5=Zabotina|first5=Olga A.|last6=Hong|first6=Mei|date=2011-02-15|title=Structure and Interactions of Plant Cell-Wall Polysaccharides by Two- and Three-Dimensional Magic-Angle-Spinning Solid-State NMR|journal=Biochemistry|volume=50|issue=6|pages=989–1000|doi=10.1021/bi101795q|pmid=21204530|s2cid=42980200 |issn=0006-2960}}</ref> She determined the binding target of the protein [[expansin]] to be hemicellulose-enriched regions of cellulose microfibrils,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=T.|last2=Park|first2=Y. B.|last3=Caporini|first3=M. A.|last4=Rosay|first4=M.|last5=Zhong|first5=L.|last6=Cosgrove|first6=D. J.|last7=Hong|first7=M.|date=2013-09-24|title=Sensitivity-enhanced solid-state NMR detection of expansin's target in plant cell walls|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=110|issue=41|pages=16444–16449|doi=10.1073/pnas.1316290110|pmid=24065828|issn=0027-8424|bibcode=2013PNAS..11016444W|pmc=3799313|doi-access=free }}</ref> thus giving insight into the mechanism of wall loosening by expansin.  

To address these questions, Hong has developed [[isotopic labeling]] strategies,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hong|first1=M.|last2=Jakes|first2=K.|date=1999-05-01|title=Selective and extensive 13C labeling of a membrane protein for solid-state NMR investigations|journal=Journal of Biomolecular NMR|language=en|volume=14|issue=1|pages=71–74|doi=10.1023/A:1008334930603|pmid=10382307|s2cid=41194972|issn=1573-5001}}</ref> [[Two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|multidimensional]] NMR correlation experiments,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hong|first=Mei|date=1999-09-01|title=Resonance assignment of 13C/15N labeled solid proteins by two- and three-dimensional magic-angle-spinning NMR|journal=Journal of Biomolecular NMR|language=en|volume=15|issue=1|pages=1–14|doi=10.1023/A:1008334204412|pmid=10549131|s2cid=1474913|issn=1573-5001}}</ref> [[Magnetization transfer|polarization transfer]] techniques,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hong|first1=Mei|last2=Schmidt-Rohr|first2=Klaus|date=2013-02-07|title=Magic-Angle-Spinning NMR Techniques for Measuring Long-Range Distances in Biological Macromolecules|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=46|issue=9|pages=2154–2163|doi=10.1021/ar300294x|pmid=23387532|issn=0001-4842|pmc=3714308}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Roos|first1=Matthias|last2=Mandala|first2=Venkata S.|last3=Hong|first3=Mei|date=2018-09-13|title=Determination of Long-Range Distances by Fast Magic-Angle-Spinning Radiofrequency-Driven 19F–19F Dipolar Recoupling NMR|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B|volume=122|issue=40|pages=9302–9313|doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.8b06878|pmid=30211552|issn=1520-6106|pmc=6314681}}</ref> and computational methods for resonance assignment of NMR spectra.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fritzsching|first1=K. J.|last2=Yang|first2=Y.|last3=Schmidt-Rohr|first3=K.|last4=Hong|first4=Mei|date=2013-04-28|title=Practical use of chemical shift databases for protein solid-state NMR: 2D chemical shift maps and amino-acid assignment with secondary-structure information|journal=Journal of Biomolecular NMR|volume=56|issue=2|pages=155–167|doi=10.1007/s10858-013-9732-z|pmid=23625364|issn=0925-2738|pmc=4048757}}</ref>
